title: UK to launch world’s first licensing scheme for knife sales
description:
Exclusive: Measures aimed at tackling grey market sellers known to sell dangerous knives to children

text: Ministers will introduce the world’s first licensing scheme for businesses and private individuals selling all types of knives including cutlery, the Home Office announced on Wednesday.
In a drive to fulfil the government’s pledge to halve knife crime within 10 years, shops and online vendors selling butter knives or machetes will be expected to apply for a licence or face fines.
Overseas sellers will be expected to use a UK-based intermediary responsible for meeting the licensing rules.
The measures are aimed at tackling the grey market – rogue and unregulated online sellers – who are known to sell dangerous knives to children.

The new regime will cover the full range of knives, the Home Office has said, unlike schemes elsewhere in the world, which target certain types. Sharp domestic kitchen knives are of particular concern because they have often been used in deadly attacks.
Ministers are planning to include homeware shops selling cutlery in the licensing scheme. Reports claimed in the spring that cutlery would be excluded from any licensing scheme.

Police will be able to take action against sellers who break the rules, including revoking licences, making it harder for rogue and grey-market sellers to supply dangerous weapons to children and criminals.
The move has been welcomed by prominent anti-knife campaigners.

Leanne Lucas, who was repeatedly stabbed whilst helping to run a Taylor Swift-themed dance class in Southport when Bebe King, six, Elsie Dot Stancombe, seven, and nine-year-old Alice Da Silva Aguiar were fatally attacked, welcomed the licensing scheme.
Axel Rudakubana, who was jailed for life for the attack, bought a large kitchen knife, used in the attack, online via Amazon.

Lucas said: “For too long, we have focused on responding to knife harm after it has happened. We need to be just as determined to prevent it in the first place. That means challenging the systems and practices that allow knives to be so easily accessible.”

Pooja Kanda, whose 16-year-old son, Ronan, was stabbed through the heart with a sword in a case of mistaken identity near their Wolverhampton home, said the new law was “an important step” towards stopping similar attacks.
“Those who sell dangerous weapons must take responsibility for where those weapons end up,” said Kanda.
The plans will draw criticism from conservation and shooting groups who have pointed out the ease with which many knives are available to gangsters and criminals in their own homes.

Police officers had warned that a proposed licensing scheme would load another responsibility upon already stretched forces. The Home Office is still to assess the full costs and administration of the scheme.
The licensing scheme, which will require legislation, follows a consultation launched in December 2025 in the wake of the Southport killings.
Since then, the government has mandated two‑step age verification for online knife purchases and required sellers to report bulk orders of six or more knives.
Each knife seller’s licence is expected to last for three years and will carry a fee set on a full-cost-recovery basis.
UK businesses will be able to obtain an import licence, and the government is exploring a combined sales and import licence for businesses requiring both.
Sellers would be subject to background and criminal record checks by police, as with firearms licensing. There could also be inspections of premises to ensure knives were being stored safely.
Retail chains selling knives would need a licence for each of their individual stores.
They face being stripped of their licence if they breach the law by selling a banned weapon, committing any other criminal offence or failing to meet conditions of their registration.
Following lobbying from antique collectors and military historians, the government is considering the case for exemptions relating to heritage collections, crafts and trades.
Forces recorded 48,615 offences involving a knife or sharp instrument in the year ending June 2026 – down 6% year-on-year, though up 49% compared to March 2016.
Officials said that the licensing scheme is expected to cover all knives but they are still considering some limited exemptions.
Sarah Jones, the policing minister, said: “If you make money selling knives, you should be responsible for making sure they are sold safely and lawfully.

“A licensing system will help us drive up standards, hold sellers accountable and make it harder for dangerous weapons to reach children and criminals. It is another important step towards our mission to halve knife crime within a decade.”
In a further development, the government has announced plans to tag thousands more offenders before they leave prison.
At present, nearly all offenders released on licence, including stalkers and perpetrators of domestic violence, leave without being electronically monitored.
It comes as further waves of offenders are set to be released early over the next year to free up prison spaces in overcrowded jails in England and Wales.
Six prisons started fitting tags before departure last year under the “tagging at source” scheme, and another 83 will follow suit by the end of March.
